measurement.happened:
This week in Russia was dominated by several major threads, and I will walk through them one by one.

THE OLESHKY CEASEFIRE AND EVACUATION. The single most prominent story of the week was the Melania Trump-brokered local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast. Beginning on October 24 and holding through the following days, the truce allowed demining operations, an aid mission, and the evacuation of starved and wounded residents who had been trapped under Russian occupation for years. By October 30 and 31, hundreds of evacuees left Oleshky by bus, crossed into Belarus, and then arrived in Ukrainian-controlled territory, where they reunited with families. BBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle, CNN, and TV5Monde all covered the emotional reunions. The ceasefire held for at least three days before the next round of strikes resumed. This was a rare moment of humanitarian progress in a grinding war, and it drew attention to the human cost of occupation. The Kremlin downplayed the event while publicly confirming the demining was complete. (Supported by headlines from Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, CNN, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, FT, CNBC, Bloomberg.)

RUSSIA-AFRICA SUMMIT AND AFRICAN STRATEGY. Putin hosted the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on October 28-29, and it was a big deal. He positioned Russia as a better, less colonial partner than the West. Concrete outcomes included: Ghana agreeing to a 2,000 MW nuclear plant backed by Rosatom; Rosatom in advanced talks with four African states on floating nuclear power plants; Rusal (Russia's aluminum giant) signing bauxite and alumina joint ventures in Ghana; Ethiopia receiving 12 Su-35 fighter jets ahead of schedule with S-400 air-defense systems to follow; and reports that Russia is widening its military recruitment drive in Africa, with 27 Ugandan citizens killed or presumed dead fighting for Russia, and at least one Malagasy soldier killed. Putin also met with Ethiopia's leadership and discussed broader security ties. The summit was widely seen as a political showcase, with TV5Monde calling it a 'vitrine politique.' (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera, CNN, Bloomberg, FT.)

G20 TENSIONS AND EUROPEAN DIPLOMACY. Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov attended the G20 foreign ministers meeting in the United States, hosted by Secretary of State Rubio. The meeting was tense: European diplomats, including Poland's representative, objected to Russia's presence, and the group family photo was cancelled. Lavrov said inviting Poland to the G20 broke diplomatic rules. EU High Representative Kallas said hosting Putin at a future G20 may normalize war crimes. Rubio defended Russia's inclusion. Meanwhile, the Pentagon reportedly told European allies to cool their rhetoric on Russia. The US and Russia also submitted rival resolutions on Western Sahara to the UN Security Council, both of which were defeated, leaving the MINURSO peacekeeping mission to expire. (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, AFP, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

NOVAYA GAZATA CLOSURE. On October 30, Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last major independent newspaper, announced it was shutting down under pressure from authorities. The paper's editors described it as an assassination, and Nobel laureate editor-in-chief Murat Sayaputov called it part of the Kremlin's 'military campaign.' The closure followed a long pattern of arrests, murder of journalists, and financial pressure. It was a significant blow to Russian independent media and drew international attention. (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, CNN, AFP, TV5Monde, FT, Bloomberg.)

UKRAINE WAR: STRIKES, REFINERIES, AND ENERGY. The war continued with high intensity. A Russian drone strike on the Dnipro train station killed at least 14 people, described as 'horrific' by Kyiv. Russia also struck Ukraine's energy grid, plunging a city into blackout. Ukraine, after pausing strikes on Russian refineries under US pressure, resumed attacks and hit a Bashneft refinery, which caught fire. Russia downed a record number of Ukrainian drones during the summit week. The UN-backed inquiry declared Russia's attacks on Ukraine's energy grid a war crime. Zelenskiy warned of new Russian ballistic missile strikes. Russia also hit Kharkiv, and a Ukrainian airstrike on a bus in Luhansk killed nine. (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, CNN, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC.)

RUSSIA'S ENERGY AND OIL TRADE. Russia extended its ban on most diesel exports through January, using quotas to fulfill a deal with the US. Three Russian diesel tankers, two of them under sanctions, steamed toward the United States. A New Jersey governor threatened to block delivery of Russian diesel cargoes. Freight rates for Russian oil stayed at record highs amid a tanker shortage and Black Sea risks. Russia turned to the Arctic WWII route to export grain as Black Sea battles raged. The shadow fleet turned to nets and rubber tires for makeshift drone armor. Gulf oil bargains lured India away from Russian crude as freight costs soared. (Supported by Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, DW, Al Jazeera.)

RUSSIA IN EUROPE: SABOTAGE, ESPIONAGE, AND DIPLOMACY. German police arrested two suspects planning sabotage attacks for Russia. Romania's president called an alleged Russian sabotage plot a 'grave violation' of NATO security, with a fire set near a weapons factory by a Russia-run network. The US Embassy warned of a mass casualty threat at a Moscow museum. The FSB said the US had warned Russia of a possible attack on Moscow. Finland and Norway held a rare phone call with Putin to discuss ending the war, though Denmark criticized them for not coordinating with allies. The CIA Director visited Moscow. A Russian detained in Poland after photographing rail infrastructure. (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, WSJ.)

RUSSIA, MUSK, AND SPACE. Putin met with Elon Musk and praised him as 'truly a genius.' The two discussed satellite coordination, and Russia is developing a Starlink alternative. Putin saluted Musk's genius as Russia plays catch-up in the satellite space. This was a notable moment of personal diplomacy between two strongmen. (Supported by Reuters, BBC, DW, CNBC, WSJ, Bloomberg.)

SPORTS AND CULTURE. The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Russia can compete in world championships, ending a ban that had kept Russia out of international ice hockey. This angered the IIHF and drew criticism. Ukraine also sanctioned the Russian cartoon 'Masha and the Bear.' (Supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Al Jazeera.)

DOMESTIC AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE. The war is straining Kremlin finances, and Putin is reaching into more pockets for new revenue. Russia added Apple and Microsoft to its state surveillance registry. Democrats in the US are probing Russian diesel and asking banks to save records. Italian taxpayers are paying millions to keep Russian yachts afloat. A Russian businessman blamed sanctions in a 30 million pound divorce battle. (Supported by AP, Bloomberg, CNN, FT, WSJ, DW.)
measurement.expected:
Based on this week's headlines, here is what I expect in Russia from November 1 to roughly November 8, 2026.

OLESHKY AFTERMATH AND HUMANITARIAN FOLLOW-UP. Almost certain: the evacuation and reunification will continue to dominate Russian and Ukrainian media, with both sides claiming credit or criticizing the process. The local ceasefire will likely lapse or be extended by a few days, and there will be political arguments in Moscow about whether to expand the truce to other occupied cities. The Kremlin will use the event to show it is capable of humanitarian gestures while maintaining its broader war position. I am almost certain this story will keep generating headlines.

G20 AND EUROPEAN DIPLOMACY. Probable: the G20 photo fiasco will fuel a week of European diplomatic maneuvering, with Brussels trying to coordinate a unified stance before any follow-up talks. The Pentagon's advice to cool rhetoric will create friction within the US alliance. I expect Rubio to issue a statement or two defending the meeting, and European foreign ministers to hold a follow-up call. The Western Sahara resolution failure will leave a gap in UN peacekeeping that both the US and Russia will try to fill with their own proposals. I am probable on continued G20-related friction.

NOVAYA GAZATA AND MEDIA LANDSCAPE. Probable: the closure of Novaya Gazeta will trigger a wave of commentary, both inside and outside Russia. I expect the Kremlin to downplay it as a business decision while independent bloggers and exiled journalists react. There may be a small protest or two in Moscow, but I would not bet on a major crackdown directly tied to the closure. The media landscape will feel noticeably thinner, and other outlets may be on notice. I am probable on sustained media coverage and some domestic reaction.

UKRAINE WAR: STRIKES AND COUNTER-STRIKES. Almost certain: the exchange of drones, missiles, and strikes on energy infrastructure will continue. Russia will likely hit more Ukrainian power plants and railways, and Ukraine will target refineries and logistics. The Dnipro train station attack will be used by Kyiv to argue for more air defense, and Russia will use the Luhansk bus strike to argue Ukraine is not protecting civilians. I expect at least one major strike with significant casualties on either side. The war is not pausing.

RUSSIA-AFRICA FOLLOW-UP. Possible: the summit commitments, especially the Ghana nuclear deal and the Ethiopia jet delivery, will generate follow-up reporting and possibly a signing ceremony or press conference. Rosatom will likely issue a statement about the floating nuclear plant talks. The Ethiopian S-400 delivery will be tracked. I am possible on specific follow-up events but not on a new major announcement.

ENERGY AND OIL. Probable: the diesel export ban extension will keep US and European politicians talking. The three sanctioned tankers heading to the US will likely generate some drama in New Jersey and at the State Department. Freight rates will stay elevated. Russia's Arctic grain shipping will be a practical challenge as weather turns. I am probable on continued energy-market headlines involving Russia.

EUROPEAN SABOTAGE AND ESPIONAGE. Possible: the German arrests and the Romanian sabotage plot will keep European security services on alert. I would not be surprised to see another small incident or arrest in a European country, but I would not bet on a major escalation. The US Embassy warning about the Moscow museum will likely be followed by a quiet security operation. I am possible on a minor follow-up incident.

US-RUSSIA CHANNELS. Possible: the CIA Director's visit to Moscow and the Kremlin aide's comment about sanctions relief for the Russian investment fund suggest back-channel talks are active. Trump said a meeting with Zelenskiy and Putin will be set up soon, so I expect some scheduling or preliminary talks to be mentioned. I am possible on a concrete step toward a trilateral meeting, but unlikely on the meeting actually happening within this week.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES:
- A sudden Russian announcement of a new missile test or nuclear exercise (possible but not strongly signaled this week).
- A major Russian cyberattack on a European country triggered by the sabotage arrests (possible).
- A surprise meeting between Putin and a European leader beyond the Nordic call (unlikely but not impossible).
- A new Russian attack on the Black Sea that hits a Turkish or Bulgarian vessel, escalating maritime tensions (possible given Bulgaria's vote and Black Sea attacks).

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON:
- A full-scale Russian offensive on a new front (no signals this week).
- A major Russian domestic protest or strike triggered by the Novaya Gazeta closure (the opposition is too fragmented and suppressed).
- A sudden change in Russian oil policy, like a full export ban or a major price cut (the trend is incremental).
- A formal US-Russia peace framework being announced (too many moving parts, too little trust).
- A Russian nuclear test or new weapon deployment (possible in the abstract but not on this timeline).
- A change of government or leadership in the Kremlin (no signals at all).
emoji_reasons: The Oleshky ceasefire and the evacuation of trapped residents was the defining humanitarian event of the week, a rare moment of peace in an otherwise grinding war.
The Russia-Africa Summit, the G20 photo fiasco, the Western Sahara UN vetoes, and the Nordic-Putin phone call all made international diplomacy the week's second major thread.
The forced closure of Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last major independent newspaper, was a landmark moment for press freedom and media in Russia.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the Oleshky ceasefire moved from a diplomatic agreement to a lived humanitarian event: hundreds of civilians left the occupied town by bus, crossed into Belarus, and reunited with families in Ukrainian territory, before the truce ended and strikes resumed. That story grew from a one-city deal into the week's most emotionally resonant headline, covered by every major outlet. A large new theme appeared that was barely present in the first photo: the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, where Putin signed nuclear, aluminum, and military deals with Ghana, Ethiopia, and others, and positioned Russia as a non-colonial great power. The closure of Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last major independent newspaper, burst into the frame as a defining domestic media story. The G20 foreign ministers meeting in the United States became a new diplomatic stage where Russia's presence provoked European objections and a cancelled group photo. The diesel deal shifted from a single tanker at sea to three tankers steaming toward the US, a New Jersey governor threatening to block delivery, and Russia extending its diesel export ban through January. Espionage and sabotage in Europe grew: Germany arrested two suspects, Romania accused Russia of a sabotage plot near a weapons factory, and the US Embassy warned of a mass-casualty threat at a Moscow museum. The military intensity held steady but shifted in flavor: Ukraine paused refinery strikes under US pressure, then resumed and hit a Bashneft refinery, while Russia struck a Dnipro train station and plunged a city into blackout. A new personal-diplomacy thread appeared with Putin meeting Elon Musk and praising him as a genius while discussing satellite coordination. The Putin-Trump-Xi summit idea, the Novatek-LNG controversy, the prisoner-exchange/Hubbard story, the Mali atrocities, and the Nestle Russian-unit story all shrank or vanished from the headlines. The central-bank rate decision was digested and no longer dominated coverage. In short, the week's center of gravity moved from the US-Ukraine-Russia trilateral track toward Russia's broader global positioning in Africa, at the G20, and in European security, while the war on the ground continued at roughly the same intensity.
delta.wind: Peace-talks preparation was rated almost certain and it did happen, but it was less visible than expected; the week was more consumed by the Oleshky evacuation, the Africa Summit, and the G20 than by shuttle diplomacy and agenda leaks. The expectation of Witkoff traveling again and Zelensky holding press conferences outlining demands was only partially met; the Kremlin's public statements were more about the Africa Summit and the G20 than about what security guarantees mean in practice. Continued military strikes were rated almost certain and came true strongly: the Dnipro train station strike, the energy-grid blackout, the Bashneft refinery fire, and the record number of drones downed all fit the prediction of at least one major strike on a large city and one significant Ukrainian operation inside Russia. The diesel-deal logistics were rated probable and materialized, but in a more contentious form than anticipated: the New Jersey governor's threat to block delivery and Russia's extension of its diesel export ban through January added a layer of friction not fully foreseen. The Oleshky evacuation was rated probable with expected logistical hiccups and at least one incident; in reality the evacuation was largely a success, with hundreds of civilians leaving and emotional reunions dominating coverage, and the ceasefire held for three or more days before resuming strikes. The tone was more positive than the prediction of competing narratives and stray shells. Espionage and intelligence incidents were rated possible and came true in greater number: two arrests in Germany, the Romanian sabotage plot, the US Embassy warning, and the Polish detention of a Russian photographer all exceeded the baseline of one more arrest or expulsion. The Putin-Trump-Xi summit was rated as possible discussion but unlikely to be scheduled, and that held: it did not dominate the week and no confirmed date emerged. Economic indicators were rated probable and appeared, but as background rather than headline: the diesel export ban, record freight rates, and the war straining Kremlin finances were present but less prominent than expected. US domestic politics were rated probable and partially played out: the New Jersey governor's threat and Democratic probing of the diesel deal fit, but the bipartisan misinformation briefing and the Putin-whisperers narrative were less visible. What came that was not expected: the Russia-Africa Summit as a major diplomatic showcase, the Novaya Gazeta closure as a defining domestic story, the G20 foreign ministers meeting with its European objections, the Musk-Putin meeting, the CAS ruling allowing Russia back in world ice hockey championships, the UN inquiry declaring Russia's energy strikes a war crime, and the shadow fleet's use of rubber tires as drone armor. The pattern of error is a consistent under-weighting of Russia's broader global and domestic moves in favor of the US-Ukraine-Russia trilateral track. The forecast assumed the next week would be dominated by the road to Abu Dhabi and the diesel tanker's arrival, but Russia used the same week to host an African summit, assert itself at the G20, close its last independent paper, and hold a personal meeting with Musk. The expectation was too tunnel-visioned on the one diplomatic thread and too optimistic that the Oleshky evacuation would be messy rather than genuinely successful.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is a simultaneous push on multiple fronts that the Kremlin is treating as a single coordinated campaign: use the humanitarian gesture at Oleshky to bank goodwill before the Abu Dhabi talks, use the Africa Summit and the G20 to build a coalition of partners and assert Russia's seat at the global table, use continued strikes on Ukraine's energy and transport to preserve leverage at the negotiating table, and use the closure of Novaya Gazeta and the tightening of domestic controls to keep the narrative tight at home. The US is the external pivot that shapes all of this: the diesel deal and the pressure to pause refinery strikes are direct American levers, and the G20 hosting by Rubio puts Russia in a room where its presence is both a prize and a provocation. The war's grinding cost is the constant substrate, draining the budget, straining the shadow fleet, and forcing creative workarounds like the Arctic grain route and rubber-tire drone armor. What ties the two photographs together is the Kremlin's attempt to look like a confident, multi-directional great power that is winning on the diplomatic and economic front even as the war grinds on, and the week's events show that attempt succeeding in some dimensions (Oleshky, Africa, G20) and failing in others (Novaya Gazeta, the energy blackout, the Dnipro train station) at roughly the same time.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A delivered a detailed, six-theme picture that was largely on target for the week's core dynamics. Its strongest hits: the Oleshky ceasefire as a confidence-building step and the dominant humanitarian story (Theme 1); the continued high-intensity mutual strikes including the Dnipro train station killing 14-15, the Bashneft refinery fire, and the record drone downings (Theme 2); the diesel tanker still en route with corporate fallout, the executive-departure scandal, and the New Jersey governor's threat (Theme 3); the broadening espionage pattern with Germany's sabotage arrests, Romania's fire near a weapons factory, and Poland detaining a Russian photographing rail infrastructure (Theme 4); the Baltic port shipping disruption and the Arctic grain rerouting (Theme 5); and Serbia's Vucic conceding defeat after his Putin-backed gamble failed (Theme 6). The 'less likely surprises' bucket was particularly well-calibrated: the corporate scandal (WSJ executive departures over undisclosed Russian funding), the North Korean labor follow-up (three separate headlines), and the Black Sea escalation (Bulgaria, Turkey warnings) all materialized. The pattern recognition of 'three in a row of small gestures' correctly anticipated that Oleshky would be the centerpiece rather than a second new ceasefire. The forecast correctly noted the tanker would not physically arrive until mid-November, matching reality. It also correctly flagged the Putin-Trump-Xi summit as an active thread producing at least one headline, which it did (Zelensky irked, Trump saying it would be set up soon). What A missed: the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow (a major scheduled event with nuclear deals, fighter jets to Ethiopia, and African recruitment), the Novaya Gazeta closure (a landmark media event), the G20 foreign ministers meeting and the cancelled photo, the Putin-Musk satellite meeting, the CAS ice hockey ruling, and the Qatar-Iran meeting in Moscow. It also slightly over-predicted a satellite close-approach follow-up and Austrian/German retaliation for prior expulsions, neither of which produced a clear headline. The central-bank and oil-tax threads were correctly flagged as recurring reference points rather than new events. Overall, A's picture of the week's center of gravity—diplomatic positioning, military intensity, energy-deal logistics, and hybrid-war broadening—was accurate, and its specific sub-predictions hit at a higher rate than they missed.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B was more concise and slightly more cautious in its probability language, and it captured the same core dynamics with comparable accuracy. Its strongest hits: the Oleshky ceasefire as the practical test of the diplomatic track, with Melania Trump visible in the story (she brokered it); the continued mutual strikes with at least one major hit on a Ukrainian city and one Ukrainian drone operation inside Russia (Dnipro station, Bashneft); the diesel deal's political fallout with congressional reaction and the tanker already at sea (correctly not expected to arrive); the espionage pattern broadening to one more European capital (Germany, Romania, Poland all produced headlines); the economic indicators being digested; and the US domestic politics thread with the bipartisan disinformation briefing. B correctly assessed the Putin-Trump-Xi summit as 'possible discussion, unlikely to be scheduled,' which matched the week's reality (Zelensky was irked, Trump said it would be set up soon, but no confirmed date). It also correctly noted that the Oleshky ceasefire was limited to one city and would not expand without a trigger. What B missed: the same major events A missed—the Russia-Africa Summit, Novaya Gazeta closure, G20 tensions, Putin-Musk meeting, CAS ruling, and Qatar-Iran meeting. It did not flag the Serbia Vucic defeat, the corporate executive-departure scandal, or the North Korean labor follow-up as specifically as A did. Its 'less likely surprises' list was shorter and less specific, missing the corporate scandal and the North Korean labor thread that both materialized. The 'things I would not bet on' list was reasonable and nothing on it happened. B's overall picture was directionally correct but less granular than A's, and it made fewer specific sub-predictions that could be scored as hits.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts shared the same core architecture: Oleshky as the diplomatic centerpiece, continued military intensity, diesel-deal logistics, espionage broadening, and economic pressure. Both correctly identified the week's center of gravity and both missed the same set of major surprises—the Russia-Africa Summit (a scheduled, high-visibility event in Moscow), the Novaya Gazeta closure, the G20 foreign ministers meeting with its cancelled photo, the Putin-Musk satellite meeting, and the CAS ice hockey ruling. These shared misses are significant and suggest both forecasters were anchored on the Ukraine-war-and-diplomacy axis and underweighted Russia's broader global outreach and domestic media politics. Where the two diverge is in specificity and the number of checkable sub-predictions. A made more granular claims: the Serbia Vucic defeat (hit), the corporate executive-departure scandal (hit), the North Korean labor follow-up (hit), the Arctic grain rerouting (hit), and the pattern of small confidence-building gestures (hit). B's predictions were more general, so while they were directionally correct, they offered fewer specific items to score. B did have a slight edge on the Putin-Trump-Xi summit probability (calling it 'unlikely to be scheduled' was more precise than A's 'at least one headline,' though both were technically correct). B also correctly named Melania Trump in the Oleshky story, which A did not do explicitly. On the espionage theme, A named specific likely countries and mechanisms, and the week delivered Germany, Romania, and Poland—matching A's broader pattern call. B's espionage prediction was vaguer ('one more arrest or diplomatic expulsion') and also correct. The 'less likely surprises' buckets are where A pulls ahead: A's list of six items produced at least four clear hits, while B's shorter list produced about two. Neither forecast was wrong in its overall shape, but A's greater specificity gave a reader a richer and more accurate map of the week. The shared blind spots (Africa, Novaya Gazeta, G20, Musk) are notable but do not distinguish the two. On balance, A's more detailed and better-calibrated set of sub-predictions, combined with its stronger pattern recognition (the 'three in a row' framing, the corporate-scandal acceleration, the espionage broadening), gives it a narrow but real edge over B's more cautious and less granular picture. VERDICT: A
